France’s Senate Rejects Rule Forcing Bitcoin Holders to Declare Self-Custody Wallets

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • France’s Senate has rejected a proposal that would have forced bitcoin holders to report self-custody wallets worth €100,000 or more to the tax authorities, along with two other crypto tax measures in the 2027 budget.
  • Industry observers note that senators voted down two identical amendments on Nov.
  • Industry observers note that the first, amendment I-2447, came from Sens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

France’s Senate has rejected a proposal that would have forced bitcoin holders to report self-custody wallets worth €100,000 or more to the tax authorities, along with two other crypto tax measures in the 2027 budget.

Industry observers note that senators voted down two identical amendments on Nov. 24 during debate on the first part of the 2027 finance bill. Both would have required taxpayers to declare crypto wallets they hold directly, outside a crypto service provider, when the total value inside reached at least €100,000 on Dec. 31 of the tax year.

Industry observers note that the first, amendment I-2447, came from Sens. Pascal Savoldelli and Pierre Barros and the Communist-led CRCE-K group. The second, amendment I-2992, came from Sen. Anne-Sophie Romagny and seven other senators. The government opposed both, and both were rejected.

It has been revealed that backers argued that France already makes taxpayers declare accounts on foreign crypto platforms, just like foreign bank accounts. Wallets that holders manage themselves, without an intermediary, escape any such obligation.

“They have become the digital equivalent of the undeclared safe,” the CRCE-K group wrote in its amendment, adding that tax authorities can’t see them, check gains on them or reach them in an estate or when a holder moves abroad.

Romagny’s version pointed to a gap in the numbers. Crypto holders in France realized €3.5 billion in gains in 2021, but only €400 million in digital assets were declared to the tax administration that same year, the amendment said. It proposed fines of up to €10,000 for failing to declare.

Recent findings suggest that the National Assembly had approved the same wallet rule on Nov. 3. It fell away the next day, when deputies rejected the entire revenue section of the budget. Senators then took up the same measure as an amendment to the budget.

It has been revealed that senators also rejected two other proposals from the CRCE-K group. Amendment I-2421 would have ended France’s tax deferral on swaps into electronic money tokens under the EU’s MiCA rules. That would have made converting bitcoin into a regulated stablecoin a taxable event.

In a recent development, amendment I-2428 would have pulled crypto into France’s exit tax on unrealized gains for people who move their tax home abroad. It counted all crypto toward the €800,000 threshold, including coins held in self-custody or outside France.

Sources indicate that david Amiel, France’s minister for public action and accounts, argued against the wallet rule, saying the EU’s DAC8 directive already puts reporting duties on crypto firms. He noted he was “more circumspect” about a “purely declarative” obligation that would not help authorities track crypto used in money laundering or tax fraud.

The Senate’s finance committee also opposed the measures, and rapporteur general Christine Lavarde recommended rejecting all three. Lavarde noted that the wallet amendments drew on a recommendation from a Senate information report filed in June, and she left the question of the threshold to the government.

Self-custody has become a sore spot in France. DAC8 reporting on crypto platforms began on Jan. 1, 2026, and Bull Bitcoin has filed a legal challenge to annul France’s DAC8 rules over privacy concerns.

Holders have also raised safety concerns. In August, bitcoiners were warned of wrench attacks after France’s tax authority confirmed a data breach affecting hundreds of thousands of people.

In a recent development, reporting rules for platforms are still expanding. The National Assembly is set to debate approval of the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, or CARF, which shares crypto tax data between countries, on Dec. 7.

It has been revealed that the wallet fight is not fully over. The Senate is still working through the 2027 budget and is set to vote on the full bill on Dec. 9, before a joint committee of both chambers takes it up.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rinnai has debuted a fresh lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.
  • The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes.
  • Heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rinnai has debuted a fresh lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

Heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

Rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

According to recent reports, the lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

Recent findings suggest that there are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

It has been revealed that the new Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

Sources indicate that an optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

Recent findings suggest that wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

The units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai says the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

It has been revealed that the series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

It has been revealed that I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

Recent findings suggest that rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

Home » Blitz news » Fidelity Crypto Adds AAVE, LINK, UNI, Expanding Asset List to Eight.

Fidelity Investments adds three DeFi tokens to its retail lineup.

Fidelity Investments has added AAVE, Chainlink (LINK) and Uniswap (UNI) to its Fidelity Crypto trading service, expanding its supported digital asset list from five to eight. The addition lifts the number of supported assets from five to eight and brings three DeFi tokens to eligible US customers.

Fidelity announced the update on its official website and in an X post. The platform now supports Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Solana (SOL), Litecoin (LTC), AAVE, LINK, UNI and the Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD), a US dollar-pegged stablecoin the company announced in January 2026.

Industry observers note that each newly introduced token is tied to a different part of DeFi. AAVE is the token for Aave, a lending protocol that mediates cryptocurrency lending and borrowing.

According to recent reports, UNI is the governance token for Uniswap, a decentralized exchange. LINK is used in Chainlink, an oracle network that delivers external information such as price data to smart contracts.

Trading and custody are handled by Fidelity Digital Assets, a subsidiary licensed as a U.S. National Trust Bank. The service is available to eligible U.S. customers aged 18 and over residing in states where Fidelity provides the service.

Fidelity rolled out Fidelity Crypto for individual investors in 2022, initially offering Bitcoin and Ether. The latest addition follows Charles Schwab’s November 9 listing of Solana, Avalanche and Chainlink on its spot crypto platform.

Fidelity’s addition of AAVE, UNI and LINK extends a major US brokerage’s retail crypto offering to DeFi infrastructure tokens. It also adds to competition among traditional brokerages for crypto-active customers, following Schwab’s recent expansion.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • US job advertisements for less-experienced workers grew more slowly at listed companies with greater estimated exposure to AI agents.
  • 23 research paper examining 34.8 million US job advertisements across 1,784 publicly listed companies found a widening gap in recruitment demand between experienced and less-experienced professionals after the release of Anthropic's Claude Code 2.0 in September 2025.
  • The researchers found that a one-standard-deviation increase in estimated exposure to AI agents was associated with 4.54% lower job posting growth for non-senior positions over the six months following the release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

US job advertisements for less-experienced workers grew more slowly at listed companies with greater estimated exposure to AI agents.

In a recent development, A Nov. 23 research paper examining 34.8 million US job advertisements across 1,784 publicly listed companies found a widening gap in recruitment demand between experienced and less-experienced professionals after the release of Anthropic's Claude Code 2.0 in September 2025.

The researchers found that a one-standard-deviation increase in estimated exposure to AI agents was associated with 4.54% lower job posting growth for non-senior positions over the six months following the release.

It has been revealed that the disparity became more pronounced when the researchers examined recruitment based on experience requirements. Positions requiring up to five years of professional experience recorded 4.87% lower posting growth associated with the same increase in AI exposure.

The study compared how estimated AI agent exposure related to ad growth by seniority and experience at sampled US listed firms.

Higher estimated exposure was linked to slower posting growth in non-senior titles and in ads asking for up to five years of experience.

In a recent development, the results concern posting growth at sampled listed firms. Exposure is estimated from stock returns and aggregate OpenRouter activity. The senior-title and six-plus-years estimates were statistically inconclusive. The analysis leaves causal effects and actual hires unresolved.

Industry observers note that table 7, Panel B, in the Nov. 23, 2026, arXiv revision. Coefficients of −4.539 and −4.868 are shown to two decimal places on a common linear scale, using the authors' approximation of percentage growth. The baseline and comparison track average monthly postings.

The results concern posting growth at sampled listed firms. Exposure is estimated from stock returns and aggregate OpenRouter activity. The senior-title and six-plus-years estimates were statistically inconclusive. The analysis leaves causal effects and actual hires unresolved.

Meanwhile, the researchers found no statistically significant relationship between AI exposure and posting growth for senior positions or roles requiring at least six years of experience.

The difference between the two groups was statistically significant, suggesting that emerging AI capabilities are affecting recruitment priorities unevenly across experience levels.

Economists Nicola Borri, Anton Cheremukhin, Yukun Liu and Aleh Tsyvinski used Anthropic's Sept. 29, 2025, Claude Code upgrade as a dividing point in their analysis. The upgrade expanded Claude's ability to work autonomously, letting it take on more complex coding tasks with less human intervention.

To estimate corporate exposure to these emerging capabilities, the researchers examined how closely companies' stock returns tracked growth in AI agent usage on OpenRouter, a platform providing access to multiple AI models.

Companies with higher exposure scores were subsequently more likely to discuss AI agents in regulatory filings and earnings calls.

The researchers found no statistically significant relationship between estimated AI exposure and job posting growth before the Claude Code upgrade. The divergence emerged in recruitment data covering October 2025 through March 2026.

The findings raise longer-term questions about how companies will develop their future workforce as AI agents become capable of performing tasks traditionally assigned to less-experienced employees.

Junior positions have historically provided workers with opportunities to develop the technical expertise, institutional knowledge, and professional judgment required for senior roles.

If companies increasingly automate that work while still demanding experienced professionals, workers entering the labor market could face fewer opportunities to gain the qualifications employers continue to seek.

That could eventually create a recruitment problem for companies themselves as they compete for experienced workers while narrowing the career pathways that produce them.

French senators on Nov. 24 rejected a proposal that would have required taxpayers to disclose self-hosted cryptocurrency holdings exceeding €100,000.

In a recent development, they would have had to report those assets as of Dec. 31.

This would have been the case even if they had held the same coins since January without making any sales.

Two matching amendments to the French 2027 budget were rejected by the Senate during the first reading of the draft.

Senators Pascal Savoldelli and Anne-Sophie Romagny reintroduced the proposal after it briefly passed in the National Assembly earlier in the month.

French taxpayers must disclose their crypto assets held on foreign crypto platforms.

According to recent reports, these amendments would have expanded disclosure requirements to wallets that owners directly control. This pertains to a wallet that is not managed by an exchange or another custodian.

The French National Assembly approved the €100,000 disclosure threshold in a 150-44 vote on Nov. 3. There were also eight abstentions.

The next day, the National Assembly voted down the entire revenue portion of the budget.

This vote brought down the wallet disclosure provision along with the rest of the budget.

However, the subsequent effort to revive the provision in the Senate was defeated.

It should be noted that the 2027 budget is still being considered at the time of writing.

The Senate also rejected two other crypto-related measures debated as part of the budget.

One was a provision to tax gains realized when holders exchange cryptocurrencies for certain stablecoins.

The second was a proposal to expand France's exit tax to include unrealized gains on cryptocurrencies held by taxpayers who move their tax residence outside the country.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.
  • And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.
  • Tesla’s official Robotaxi account revealed the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account revealed the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

Recent findings suggest that the order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

According to recent reports, the subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print states “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”.

It has been revealed that the email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”.

Sources indicate that the rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and notes you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”.

In a recent development, musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

It has been revealed that tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

In a recent development, railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

Sources indicate that I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

Recent findings suggest that and here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” presently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a upcoming two-seater that can do nothing else.

It has been revealed that if the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The bitcoin price fell to near $57,500 on Wednesday morning, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data, as Wall Street opened sharply lower on a deepening technology selloff, hotter-than-expected core inflation and a fresh round of U.S.
  • Bitcoin slipped to $60,000 on Tuesday morning and lost that level later in the day.
  • It has been revealed that the world’s largest cryptocurrency is down about 24% in November and on course for its worst month since 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bitcoin price fell to near $57,500 on Wednesday morning, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data, as Wall Street opened sharply lower on a deepening technology selloff, hotter-than-expected core inflation and a fresh round of U.S. tariff proposals. Bitcoin had traded near $58,400 before the 8:30 a.m. ET data release.

Bitcoin slipped to $60,000 on Tuesday morning and lost that level later in the day. It has now given back all of Monday’s spike above $64,000, which faded within hours after Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO. The bitcoin price remains above the weekend low near $55,100, its lowest level in more than two years.

It has been revealed that the world’s largest cryptocurrency is down about 24% in November and on course for its worst month since 2022. It has also lost more than 30% since the start of the year, as record ETF outflows, rising rate-hike bets and a slide in AI stocks have kept buyers on the sidelines.

It has been revealed that the selling spread from Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi fell 6.16% overnight, to Wall Street. The Nasdaq Composite tumbled about 4% in early trading, while the S&P 500 fell about 3% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost about 2%. Nvidia sank more than 8% to near $142, and Micron and AMD each fell more than 9% as doubts over the returns on AI spending resurfaced.

Tariffs added to the risk-off mood. The Trump administration proposed fresh Section 301 tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan and India, over what it calls excess industrial capacity. China faces a 20% duty on top of the 25% imposed in 2018, CNBC reported. The new duties would take effect after a public comment period, in January at the earliest.

Inflation came in hotter than expected. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 0.3% in October and 3.8% from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy and is the Fed’s preferred gauge, climbed 3.3% from a year ago, above the 3.2% economists had expected and up from 3.1% in September.

It has been revealed that growth also ran hot. Real gross domestic product increased at a 4.3% annual rate in the third quarter, the Bureau of Economic Analysis noted in its second estimate, up from the 3.4% pace first reported. Reuters called it the fastest growth in three years, driven by consumer spending and business investment in AI.

The reports solidified bets on another rate increase, with traders pricing in a 98% chance of a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting. The 10-year Treasury yield fell more than 6 basis points to 4.84% as investors bought bonds for protection, but that offered little support to the bitcoin price.

ETF selling continues. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $231.6 million on Tuesday, less than half of Monday’s $569.7 million, their sixth straight session of outflows. November withdrawals reached about $4.94 billion through Nov. 24, putting the funds on course for their worst month since launching in January 2024.

Crypto stocks fell with the broader market. Strategy (MSTR) dropped about 8% to near $71 in early trading, after closing down 8.12% at $77.55 on Tuesday. MSCI is set to remove the company from its indexes on Nov. 30, and Monness, Crespi, Hardt & Co. cut its price target to $59. The bitcoin price now sits well below Strategy’s average purchase price of $75,446.

Coinbase (COIN) fell about 6% to near $96, while Robinhood (HOOD) lost nearly 6% and Circle (CRCL) slid more than 7%. Miners took heavier hits. IREN dropped about 11% and CleanSpark (CLSK) fell nearly 10%, while Riot Platforms (RIOT), which sold thousands of bitcoin earlier this month, was down nearly 8%.

U.S. stock and bond markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and reopen Friday for a half-day session, making Wednesday the last full trading day of the week. Investors will next look to the November jobs report on Dec. 4, the last major data point before the Fed’s rate decision on Dec. 9.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $57,500.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) kept leaving crypto exchanges this week as the price of the meme cryptocurrency fell to levels last seen in the spring of 2021, and on Wednesday, the outflow picked up sharply.

Recent findings suggest that according to CoinGlass data, 520.83 billion SHIB left exchanges over the past 24 hours. That amount made up most of the 757.51 billion SHIB that exchanges lost over the past seven days, and over the past 30 days, the outflow reached 2.88 trillion SHIB.

According to recent reports, on Wednesday evening, SHIB was trading at $0.00000344, according to CoinGlass. So far this week, the token was down 4.78%, and its market capitalization went down to $2.02 billion, according to TradingView.

According to recent reports, according to the weekly chart on TradingView, SHIB last traded at these levels in the spring of 2021, months before the token reached its all-time high of $0.00008845 on Oct. 28, 2021.

From early 2026 until mid-November, the price of SHIB held above $0.000004, and the yearly low stood at $0.00000411 at the July 17 close. In November, SHIB fell to $0.00000373, and in late November, the token dropped as low as $0.00000337. On Jan. 1, the token closed the day at $0.00000692, and since the start of the year, SHIB has lost 50.3% of its value, according to CoinGlass. As of Nov. 22, SHIB had lost 22.7% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

The latest drop in SHIB came after Bitcoin fell back below $60,000 this week. On Saturday, Nov. 21, Bitcoin dropped as low as $55,150, its lowest price since September 2024. Over the past 24 hours, $57,590 worth of SHIB futures positions were liquidated, and $54,750 of that amount came from long positions on OKX, according to CoinGlass.

The Wednesday outflow was not the first large one this month. On Nov. 17, about 312 billion SHIB were withdrawn from exchanges, according to CryptoQuant. On the same day, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million, according to Etherscan.

CoinGlass data also highlights that since late 2024, the total SHIB balance on exchanges has gone down by 19.18 trillion tokens, or 20.54%, to 74.19 trillion, and over the same period, the price of SHIB fell by 88.39%. The remaining 74.19 trillion SHIB on exchanges make up 12.59% of the circulating supply and are worth about $254.75 million.

Most of the 24-hour outflow came from exchanges that CoinGlass groups as "Others," as their combined SHIB balance fell by 88.5% to 70.93 billion tokens. Over the same period, the SHIB balances of Binance and OKX barely changed, and Coinbase, Bitfinex and Bitstamp added SHIB.

As a result, in the week when the price of SHIB fell to levels last seen in 2021, exchanges lost more SHIB in a single day than over the previous six days combined, according to CoinGlass data.

  • One in five Australian cryptocurrency investors would consider borrowing against their digital assets rather than selling them, as upcoming tax changes push holders to rethink their financial strategies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home » Crypto Market News » Australian Crypto Investors Turn to Loans Ahead of 2027 Tax Reform.

Upcoming capital gains tax reforms are prompting crypto holders to reconsider how they access cash without selling their digital assets.

One in five Australian cryptocurrency investors would consider borrowing against their digital assets rather than selling them, as upcoming tax changes push holders to rethink their financial strategies.

A survey commissioned by digital asset wealth platform Nexo found that 22.7% of Australian crypto holders would consider borrowing against their holdings instead of selling, compared with 10% of other investors.

The findings come as Australia prepares to overhaul its capital gains tax (CGT) system from July 1, 2027.

Nexo surveyed 1,000 Australian investors this October to examine how major expenses and rising living costs affect investment decisions.

The results suggest that crypto holders are more inclined to avoid selling their investments when they need additional funds.

Beyond the 22.7% considering borrowing, another 19.7% said they had delayed or decided against selling their crypto holdings.

In a recent development, crypto investors can borrow against their existing holdings instead of selling them for cash. This allows them to access money while keeping their Bitcoin or other digital assets, and potentially benefit if their value increases.

It has been revealed that the trend comes against a broader backdrop of financial pressure. According to the survey, 29.4% of all investors had delayed, reduced or cancelled a major purchase or financial strategy over the previous 12 months.

The upcoming CGT reform is another factor investors may need to consider.

Under Australia’s current system, eligible individuals, trusts and partnerships can receive a 50% capital gains tax discount on assets held for more than 12 months.

From July 1, 2027, this discount will be replaced by cost base indexation and a 30% minimum tax on eligible gains.

Under transitional arrangements, gains accrued before that date will remain eligible for the existing 50% discount, while gains accumulated afterward will be subject to the new rules.

Crypto ownership in Australia is at a record high, with 2.79 million Australians holding or trading cryptocurrency, according to the figures cited in an Australian investor Study.

That equals about 24% of the country’s 11.5 million investors, up from roughly 15% in 2023, making crypto as widely held as exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

As ownership expands, the demand for financial products that allow investors to access liquidity without selling their holdings could also increase.

Consequently, as their holdings rise in value, more investors may look for ways to cover major expenses without selling their crypto.

Industry observers note that the upcoming CGT rules could make some investors think twice before selling crypto that has increased in value. As a result, more holders may consider borrowing against their holdings to cover major expenses without having to sell their assets and potentially trigger a capital gains tax bill.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging.
  • Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has swiftly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a massive difference.
  • When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has swiftly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a massive difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

Recent findings suggest that USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely newly introduced, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the tech giant’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

Sources indicate that the ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Sources indicate that of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

According to recent reports, instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Sources indicate that heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

According to recent reports, plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It has been revealed that it may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

Sources indicate that and that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

It has been revealed that of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as rapidly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

Industry observers note that USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road swiftly.

In a recent development, but having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

In a recent development, for years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

In a recent development, now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner.
  • Six days after Nvidia’s board chair told investors “the Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” the board voted unanimously to reinstate him as president, CEO and director, effective immediately.
  • In a recent development, nvidia shares rose 33% to around $167, adding roughly a trillion dollars of market value in a session.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

Six days after Nvidia’s board chair told investors “the Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” the board voted unanimously to reinstate him as president, CEO and director, effective immediately.

In a recent development, nvidia shares rose 33% to around $167, adding roughly a trillion dollars of market value in a session. Huang’s personal net worth climbed about $36.6 billion on his 3.5% stake, moving him to 13th on the Forbes global list. Short sellers took roughly $12.2 billion in paper losses, their worst single day since at least 2019, which wiped out the $10.5 billion they had booked the prior week.

Industry observers note that the stock market absolutely ripped on the news. The Nasdaq closed up 6.51% at 24,089, its best day since April 2025. The S&P gained 4.7%, the Dow was +3%, and the VIX collapsed 25.8% to 26.62.

In a recent development, bitcoin went along with the ride—for a few hours. It touched $63,929 intraday, up 5.1%, then spent the afternoon handing it back and finished near $61,000, barely up on the day. The ETFs used the pump to exit more, with BTC ETFs seeing another $570M in outflows on the day.

ETH and other majors also closed red. Alts gave back their gains. And the CMC top 20 index managed just 0.20% gain.

That’s a 19 to 1 ratio between what the Nasdaq captured and what Bitcoin kept, on the same catalyst, on the same day. Pain for the crypto bulls.

What makes it even more painful, is that crypto fell with AI stocks the whole way down, and the standard explanation was that both trade on the same liquidity and the same risk appetite. Monday tested that and the correlation fell through. The AI trade got a catalyst and markets bounced. Crypto didn’t bounce with it.

As for Nvidia’s reversal decision itself, questions remain to say the least. The board states it was satisfied with Huang’s “candor and ability to lead,” and that input from senior U.S. officials left it confident his return “poses no national security risk.” Trump publicly pushed for it and said the board had sought assurance on the espionage allegations. What actually changed between November 17 and November 23 hasn’t been explained. The independent directors’ investigation is still open, and Nvidia is now standing up a board committee for national security and export-control oversight plus recruiting a chief compliance officer.

Perhaps answers will trickle out over time. The AI trade may not need them anyway. And crypto, well, it's in its own world right now, waiting for its own catalysts (likely quantum-related). But it’s very unclear that catalyst is coming in 2026, and it’s becoming clear that many are not interested in waiting for the answers….

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested.
  • And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.
  • The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the firm started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the firm started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

Industry observers note that that personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Recent findings suggest that then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Sources indicate that tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make right now, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab rolls out on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

Recent findings suggest that you don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:.

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold.

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if owners join the network.

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

According to recent reports, and the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no newly introduced revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Visa is testing how AI agents can use traditional banking credentials to qualify for paid work that settles in stablecoins.
  • 22, Visa Crypto Labs head Cuy Sheffield unveiled an revision to the manufacturer's Visa CLI wallet that allows users to verify their AI agents and access paid assignments on Taskmarket, a marketplace for AI-generated work.
  • The initiative expands Visa's experiments in agentic commerce beyond enabling AI systems to spend money on behalf of their owners.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Visa is testing how AI agents can use traditional banking credentials to qualify for paid work that settles in stablecoins.

On Nov. 22, Visa Crypto Labs head Cuy Sheffield unveiled an revision to the manufacturer's Visa CLI wallet that allows users to verify their AI agents and access paid assignments on Taskmarket, a marketplace for AI-generated work.

The initiative expands Visa's experiments in agentic commerce beyond enabling AI systems to spend money on behalf of their owners.

Under the new arrangement, agents can generate income by completing tasks, with payments made in Open USD, a dollar-denominated stablecoin, on the Tempo blockchain.

The service is currently available by invitation to eligible US owners, who must register a personal Visa card and authenticate it using a one-time code from their issuing bank.

Once an owner authorizes an agent, Visa registers its public signing key in the company's Agent Directory, allowing participating platforms to verify its credentials.

Recent findings suggest that taskmarket uses that directory to authenticate agents when they claim assignments or submit completed work. New jobs posted through Visa require verified agents by default, although requesters can remove that restriction.

The arrangement gives Visa a role in determining which AI agents qualify for economic opportunities while blockchain infrastructure handles their earnings.

Industry observers note that taskmarket introduced settlements on Tempo on Oct. 22, expanding its marketplace beyond USDC-denominated assignments on Coinbase's Base network. Its Visa-linked worker verification feature is currently exclusive to Tempo.

Visa automatically screens assignments before agents can undertake them. Owners running agents on their own computers can authorize them to claim and submit screened tasks without individual approval, while remotely hosted agents require human authorization.

Payments are typically released when requesters accept completed assignments, with the proceeds transferred directly to the agent owner's Tempo wallet.

Sources indicate that the owner’s bank confirms an eligible Visa card. Taskmarket checks the agent’s registered key for gated work. Payment follows a separate decision.

Both release routes send Open USD to the owner’s wallet on Tempo.

The diagram covers gated Visa CLI work on Taskmarket.

Maps Visa CLI’s documented card and directory checks and Taskmarket’s verified-worker requirement on Tempo, then contrasts the two documented payment-release routes.

The diagram covers gated Visa CLI work on Taskmarket.

Owners also retain control over settlement decisions when requesters fail to review submitted work before the deadline.

By using cardholder authentication to qualify agents for work that pays in stablecoins, Visa is testing a model in which its verification infrastructure can support economic activity that settles outside its traditional card network.

The invitation-only rollout will test whether those credentials can gain traction among businesses and individuals commissioning AI-generated work.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew Webley, CEO of The Smarter Web Company, mentioned that Bitcoin's drop has been sharper than he had anticipated, but he does not think the digital asset's price will decline much further.

The British CEO, whose tech giant recently added 55 BTC to its treasury, said investors' opinions on Bitcoin can shift considerably without any changes to Bitcoin itself.

Recent findings suggest that "Sentiment towards Bitcoin can change very quickly. Without Bitcoin changing at all," Webley noted on X.

Recent findings suggest that webley advised investors to consider Bitcoin's movements relative to other assets. Bitcoin's price decline indicates investors how much the cryptocurrency has lost in absolute terms.

It has been revealed that however, Bitcoin's performance relative to the broader market may indicate BTC is being sold specifically or whether investors are taking profits across multiple markets. Webley did not specify which assets he was comparing Bitcoin against.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CleanSpark has begun selling Bitcoin from its treasury to finance acquisitions as the company accelerates its expansion into artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Sources indicate that during the tech giant's Nov. 24 earnings call, President and CFO Gary Vecchiarelli remarked CleanSpark had sold some of its Bitcoin holdings since the end of September to strengthen its cash position ahead of anticipated acquisitions.

“We've sold some Bitcoin to pad the balance sheet with cash to prepare for some acquisitions that we expect to make in the near future.”.

Vecchiarelli added that CleanSpark could sell additional Bitcoin or borrow against its holdings to finance acquisitions without diluting existing shareholders. The company also intends to sell virtually all newly mined Bitcoin to fund daily operations.

CleanSpark ended September with approximately $1.3 billion in reported liquidity, comprising $204.8 million in cash and cash equivalents and approximately $1.13 billion in Bitcoin holdings and related exposure.

The tech giant reported exposure equivalent to 13,530 BTC at fiscal year-end but has not disclosed how much Bitcoin it subsequently sold.

The treasury strategy comes as deteriorating Bitcoin mining economics weigh on CleanSpark's financial performance.

According to its fiscal 2026 results, annual revenue declined 25% to $576.5 million, while the organization recorded a net loss of $987.1 million, compared with net income of $364 million a year earlier.

Vecchiarelli attributed approximately two-thirds of the earnings reversal to noncash adjustments in the value of its Bitcoin holdings.

Sources indicate that however, profitability also deteriorated across its mining operations. Annual gross margins contracted from 55% to 41% as the average value of mined Bitcoin fell from approximately $97,600 to $79,500.

The decline occurred despite improvements in fleet efficiency and a reduction in electricity costs from $0.057 to $0.055 per kilowatt-hour.

Against this backdrop, CleanSpark is directing more capital toward AI data centers and acquiring land and power infrastructure.

The firm secured a 20-year, $6.6 billion lease with an investment-grade tenant at its Sandersville facility in Georgia and raised $2.276 billion through secured notes to fully fund the project's development. It also expanded its Texas infrastructure portfolio through acquisitions supporting up to 885 MW of power capacity.

Vecchiarelli said management sees further acquisition opportunities as a better use of available capital than repurchasing CleanSpark shares, despite believing its stock is undervalued.

While Bitcoin provides CleanSpark with an alternative to equity financing, the cryptocurrency's recent decline has reduced the collateral value supporting its existing borrowing.

CleanSpark's annual filing showed that it had borrowed $90 million through a $100 million revolving credit facility with Two Prime Lending as of Sept. 30.

The tech giant pledged 1,665 BTC worth $139.1 million at the time, giving the loan a loan-to-value ratio of approximately 65%.

Under the agreement, a ratio exceeding 74% triggers a margin call, while liquidation can occur above 80%. Based on the September loan balance and collateral, those thresholds correspond to Bitcoin prices of approximately $73,046 and $67,568, respectively.

It has been revealed that with Bitcoin trading near $59,000 on Nov. 25, the same collateral would be worth approximately $98.2 million, pushing the loan-to-value ratio to nearly 92% if the position remained unchanged.

The miner reported $90 million outstanding and 1,665 BTC pledged to Two Prime at Sept. 30.

As Bitcoin falls, the same loan balance takes up a larger share of the pledged coins’ value.

The illustration holds Sept. 30 principal and pledged coins fixed. The current debt balance, pledged coin count, lender valuation and any lender action remain unknown.

In a recent development, loan-to-value is principal divided by collateral value. The reported Sept. 30 ratio uses $139.128 million in collateral. Each boundary price is $90 million divided by the product of 1,665 BTC and the threshold ratio. The $59,000 case values the collateral at 1,665 × $59,000. Prices are rounded to dollars and ratios to whole percentages.

Recent findings suggest that the illustration holds Sept. 30 principal and pledged coins fixed. The current debt balance, pledged coin count, lender valuation and any lender action remain unknown.

CleanSpark has not disclosed whether it has subsequently increased its collateral or reduced its outstanding debt.

Shareholders will also have less frequent visibility into those decisions after CleanSpark discontinued monthly operational updates in favor of quarterly reporting.

Its next quarterly disclosure could reveal how much of its Bitcoin treasury the company has committed to financing its AI expansion and whether additional acquisitions will require further sales or borrowing.

  • "Historically, people rotate out of it to take advantage of a massive IPO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that "Bitcoin investors tend to sell BTC when there's a substantial IPO. Then they come back.".

That's Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong's take on Bitcoin investor behavior, less than a week after the record-breaking $93.5 billion IPO of Claude creator Anthropic.

"Historically, people rotate out of it to take advantage of a massive IPO. Then they come back in," Armstrong wrote on X earlier today.

Sources indicate that the limited window of opportunity to invest in an IPO helps explain the behavior Armstrong described. For an investor to buy at the IPO price, there's only a certain period during which they can request an allocation of shares. After that, the price is determined by the market.

On Nov. 19, Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq, and that brief window of opportunity mattered.

Shares were priced at $83, up from the $70-$78 range indicated just two days earlier. Anthropic's stock, trading under the ticker ANT, opened at $111.50.

If you bought at that opening price, you paid about 34% more per share than an investor who received an allocation at the IPO price.

In a recent development, when the IPO closed on Nov. 20, 1.127 billion shares had been sold, including 147 million additional shares purchased by underwriters exercising their option.

Of the $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, Anthropic itself received around $91.6 billion. The rest went to existing shareholders.

There was also a separate $26 billion private placement involving investors such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and others. In total, the combined transactions were valued at $119.5 billion.

As for the longer-term case for holding BTC, Armstrong's point concerns investors' expectations about the future purchasing power of their money.

"If you think there is going to be more inflation and money printing in the future, bitcoin is as important as ever.".

At the heart of the matter is Bitcoin's 21 million supply limit.

It has been revealed that if you expect governments to continue expanding the money supply, you may still be excited by the prospect of a major IPO. And you may sell some of your BTC to participate in it.

Armstrong's argument is that the window of opportunity to participate in a major IPO eventually closes.

However, the reasons investors bought Bitcoin in the first place may remain long after the newly listed stock starts trading.

Check your ego at the door: Stellantis’ upcoming electric dolly turns ANY car into a tow rig

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.
  • Industry observers note that originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No.
  • In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a massive tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

Industry observers note that originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a massive tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

In a recent development, to be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow customers to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

Industry observers note that there are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

Sources indicate that okay, I like this idea and appreciate the problem it is trying to solve, but it has the same challenge as any electric-tow situation, which is the charging logistics. Even if you find a pull-through charger (very rare), if you are using an EV, you still need to charge two "vehicles," so you have to charge your car, then pull up and charge the dolly afterwards. Even if you are using a gas car, charging the dolly will be logistically challenging. Of course, that's a problem with an easy solution (more pull-through chargers), but also one that doesn't seem to be on any charging network's radar.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

$20K Nissan NX7 PHEV goes on sale with nearly 200 miles of electric range

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its new NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.
  • When the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its new NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

When the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The tech giant’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The fresh Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The fresh NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

Sources indicate that on top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

Power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

Sources indicate that why is this article written like it will be available in the US market? It’s made in China and has Chinese software, we’ll never see it.

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the latest NX7 in the comments, today.

China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong.
  • Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t the plane’s first flight.
  • Sources indicate that the CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC indicates every system worked normally.

Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

Sources indicate that the CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

The CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

The program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC indicated a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

The obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL rolled out its aviation unit.

CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and stated it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither manufacturer has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

Recent findings suggest that COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, New York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

Industry observers note that for years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

Now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

And this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

In a recent development, china also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Next Technology Holding (Nasdaq: NXTT) sold about 500 bitcoin last week and said it will put the money toward artificial intelligence projects, the latest public organization to trim its bitcoin treasury as prices slide.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Japan-based software firm disclosed in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Tuesday that it sold the coins on Nov.
  • In a recent development, the sale leaves NXTT with 5,333 BTC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Next Technology Holding (Nasdaq: NXTT) sold about 500 bitcoin last week and said it will put the money toward artificial intelligence projects, the latest public organization to trim its bitcoin treasury as prices slide.

Recent findings suggest that the Japan-based software firm disclosed in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Tuesday that it sold the coins on Nov. 21 for about $29.22 million. That works out to an average price of $58,468.11 per bitcoin, net of fees and expenses.

In a recent development, the sale leaves NXTT with 5,333 BTC. The company was paid in tether (USDT), the dollar-pegged stablecoin, rather than in dollars.

NXTT mentioned it plans to use the proceeds for research and development of its AI-related initiatives, including its AI software products and services, as well as for general corporate purposes.

It has been revealed that the sale is the first under a program the firm’s board approved on Oct. 30. That program allows NXTT to sell or pledge its bitcoin “from time to time in one or more tranches,” through exchange sales, block trades or loans that use the coins as collateral, with the stated aim of “reducing risk exposure and enhancing liquidity.”.

According to recent reports, the filing also repeats a line from the company’s latest quarterly report that marks a clear break from its earlier approach. NXTT “does not presently expect to purchase additional Bitcoin,” the company said, adding that it has adjusted its strategy to focus on managing the coins it already holds.

The program has no expiration date and doesn’t require the tech giant to sell any set amount. The board can change, pause or end it at any time. As of Nov. 24, NXTT said it had not pledged any of its bitcoin as collateral.

NXTT, which is incorporated in Wyoming but based in Saitama Prefecture, Japan, describes itself as running two strategies: AI-enabled software development and holding bitcoin. It keeps substantially all of its coins with Japan-based institutional custodians, according to its quarterly filing.

According to recent reports, the firm held 833 BTC at the end of 2024 and added 5,000 BTC in 2025, bringing its total to 5,833 BTC. Its filing puts the cost basis of those coins at about $183.1 million, or roughly $31,400 per bitcoin, meaning last week’s sale still came in well above what the company paid on average.

Industry observers note that falling prices have still hit the books. NXTT reported a net loss of $32.2 million for the first nine months of 2026, compared with net income of $295.1 million a year earlier. The firm stated the swing came mainly from a drop in the fair value of its digital assets.

According to recent reports, the tech giant has also been reshaping its leadership around AI. Earlier this month it named Chan Phang Chuen, a former platform architect focused on computing infrastructure and AI inference, as chief technical officer after Hongliang Liu resigned from the role.

It has been revealed that NXTT joins a growing list of public companies selling bitcoin to fund other businesses. Ionic Digital sold 737 bitcoin this month to pay for a data center buildout, and Rumble sold two-thirds of its bitcoin as its AI cloud business delivered its first profitable quarter.

According to recent reports, miners have been selling too. Bitdeer sold all 281 bitcoin it mined last week and now holds none. Not every treasury company is stepping back, though. Strategy added 457 bitcoin for $29.6 million during the same week NXTT was selling.

Bitcoin has struggled to hold $60,000 this week amid heavy outflows from U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs, and NXTT sold its coins near those levels.

The tech giant said the proceeds from any future sales or pledges will depend on market conditions and the timing of execution.
